name: Disguise Glasses
description: A joke about looking smart while being sneaky. The disguised face with fake glasses and mustache pairs with actual glasses to suggest someone is pretending to be intellectual or trying to look intelligent while hiding something.
meaning: 🥸👓 plays with the contrast between the obvious fake disguise and the nerd-chic signal of real glasses. It reads as 'I'm pretending to be smart/intellectual while doing something undercover or suspicious,' or 'acting like I know what I'm talking about when I don't.' The combo lands as ironic and self-aware humor.
examples: me pretending to understand the group chat discourse 🥸👓
walking into a meeting i didn't prepare for 🥸👓
my linkedin photo vs how i actually look 🥸👓
fake it till you make it energy 🥸👓
me explaining why i haven't done my homework yet 🥸👓
seoDescription: What does 🥸👓 mean? It's a self-aware joke about faking expertise or pretending to be smarter than you are while being obviously caught.

longForm.overview:
🥸👓 is the 'I'm faking it' combo. The disguised face is already ridiculous—a literal cartoon mask with a fake nose and mustache—and pairing it with glasses (the universal symbol of intelligence and studiousness) creates a joke about pretending to be smarter or more competent than you actually are. The combo does not land as genuine deception; it reads as self-aware and playful, like you are in on the joke about your own bluff.

The two emojis work because they contradict each other. Glasses suggest genuine intellectual credibility and nerd-chic authenticity. The disguise face undermines that immediately by announcing that you are wearing a cartoon mask. Together they say: 'I know this looks official, but I am obviously making this up as I go.' It is the emoji version of putting on reading glasses you do not need and nodding seriously while someone explains something you do not understand.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
🥸👓 shows up when someone wants to admit they are bluffing without actually admitting it. You send it after making a confident statement you are not entirely sure about, before walking into a situation you are unprepared for, or when someone catches you talking about something you clearly do not know. It also lands on posts about faking expertise online—LinkedIn profiles, job interviews where you oversold yourself, or group chats where you are pretending to follow an inside joke.

The combo performs well in self-roasting contexts, especially around work, school, or social situations where there is pressure to seem like you have it together. It softens the admission because the emojis are silly and the sender is laughing at themselves. It is not a deflection; it is a pre-emptive confession that you are obviously out of your depth but doing your best anyway.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Skip 🥸👓 if you are actually trying to seem credible. The combo undermines itself by design—it announces that you are faking, which defeats the purpose of faking. Avoid it in professional contexts where you genuinely need to project confidence, like a first interview, a pitch, or a client-facing moment where the stakes are real.

Also avoid 🥸👓 when the person you are talking to is not in on the self-aware humor. If someone asks you a serious question and you reply with this combo, they might think you are mocking them or that you are not taking the conversation seriously. Use it only when the sender and receiver both understand that the joke is on you, not on them.
longForm.howToReply:
Mirror 🥸👓 with a laugh if the sender is clearly roasting themselves. A simple 'lol same' or 'at least you tried' keeps the playful energy going and reassures them that everyone wings it sometimes. If the combo lands on something that actually matters—a work question or a real concern—reply with something that gently takes the conversation seriously: 'you probably know more than you think' or 'we can figure it out together.'

If someone sends 🥸👓 in a group chat about a topic you were all confused about, reply with something that normalizes the collective bluffing: 'honestly none of us know what's happening' or 'welcome to the club.' If the combo is being used to dodge accountability on something that actually went wrong, a gentle push usually works: 'jokes aside, what happened?' signals that you want the real story without calling them out.

faqs.question: What does 🥸👓 mean in a group chat
faqs.answer: It means the sender is admitting they do not actually know what everyone is talking about but are pretending to follow along. It is a self-aware joke that lands as 'I have no idea what I'm doing here' without actually derailing the conversation.

faqs.question: Is 🥸👓 flirty
faqs.answer: No. The combo is self-deprecating humor, not flirtation. If you send it to someone you like, it reads as you making fun of yourself, not as a romantic signal. Stick to different emojis if you are trying to flirt.

faqs.question: Can I use 🥸👓 to make fun of someone else
faqs.answer: Not really. The combo only works when the sender is laughing at themselves. Sending it at someone else reads as mocking rather than playful, and it will land badly. Use it only when you are the one admitting to the bluff.

faqs.question: Does 🥸👓 work on a resume or job application
faqs.answer: Absolutely not. The combo is explicitly about faking credibility, so it would only undermine your actual qualifications. Save it for personal messages and casual contexts where self-deprecating humor is welcome.

conversationExamples.message: just got assigned to lead the project meeting tomorrow 🥸👓
conversationExamples.interpretation: The sender is nervous and admitting they do not feel qualified to lead, but they are doing it anyway. They are being vulnerable in a work-appropriate way. Respond with encouragement that acknowledges the nerves: 'you've got this' or 'you'll do great, you know more than you think.'

conversationExamples.message: me explaining to my parents why i'm still in school 🥸👓
conversationExamples.interpretation: The sender is making fun of themselves for not having their life together yet. They are inviting commiseration and shared humor about being lost. Reply with matching self-roast: 'same energy' or 'at least you have a plan.'

conversationExamples.message: pretending to be interested in that thing you talked about 🥸👓
conversationExamples.interpretation: The sender is joking about themselves, admitting they were faking engagement to impress you. This is playful honesty, not a real confession. Respond with humor that shows you were not fooled: 'I could tell' or 'we can just talk about whatever.'

conversationExamples.message: giving my little cousin advice like i have my life figured out 🥸👓
conversationExamples.interpretation: The sender is being self-aware about offering guidance they are not sure about themselves. They are acknowledging the funny position of being looked up to while still figuring things out. Reply with something warm: 'still counts if it helps' or 'better fake it for them.'

conversationExamples.message: my linkedin headline vs my actual job duties 🥸👓
conversationExamples.interpretation: The sender is making a joke about the gap between how they present professionally online and what they actually do day-to-day. It is relatable commentary on personal branding. Engage with 'what's the real title' or share your own version of the gap.
